title: Build AI Agents to Automate Your Workflows
purpose: Instructor-led O’Reilly template companion with trial onboarding, editable teaching diagrams, cited notes, and universal decision exercises.

slides.title:
Build AI Agents
to Automate
Your Workflows
lines: Microsoft Copilot Studio
Tim Warner | September 8, 2026
slides.notes: Today you are the maker. We are building an AZ-900 study assistant for a Contoso colleague learning Azure fundamentals. We will improve that same assistant throughout the class. First it has a clear job. Then it uses a reference, holds a teaching conversation, calls a bounded tool, and earns a pilot decision. The Azure subject keeps our examples consistent. The design skills transfer to your own training, help desk, and internal knowledge work. No learner coding is required.

slides.title: The four course outcomes
lines: Plan a Copilot Studio agent from persona, job-to-be-done, instructions, topic map, guardrails, and success metrics.
Build a grounded AZ-900 study assistant using knowledge sources, topics, generative answers, and test prompts.
Extend the agent with actions, agent flows, MCP and subagent concepts, and human handoff patterns.
Evaluate, publish, observe, and govern the agent using analytics, agent evaluations, Power Platform Well-Architected guidance, and security principles.
slides.notes: These are the advertised outcomes. I will build the same assistant through the four modules and show the evidence for each change. Everyone can take part in short prediction, diagnosis, and decision exercises without tenant access. If your account is ready, you may explore along with the demonstration. We will show how to start a trial, but account approval is not a prerequisite for participating today. The supplied lab steps support independent practice after class. Watching the build develops understanding; independent authoring is a follow-up practice task.

slides.title: A maker and a learner
lines: You: design the assistant
Contoso colleague: learn Azure
Shared need: useful practice with a source
slides.notes: Contoso is a fictional internal training scenario. Our user has twenty or thirty minutes to study and needs help with unfamiliar cloud concepts. Our maker is responsible for the quality of that experience. The assistant explains a narrow concept, asks an original practice question, waits, and gives feedback. It can retrieve an authored study session. It cannot book an exam, know a personal appointment, or promise a pass. The illustration is conceptual, not a product screenshot or an actual customer.

slides.title: The agent’s building blocks
lines: User message through a channel
Generative orchestration
Knowledge: reference material
Topic: authored conversation
Tool: a defined operation
slides.notes: Read the diagram from the user message toward the capabilities. A channel carries the conversation. A trigger starts work. With generative orchestration, descriptions help the agent select knowledge, topics, and tools; it may select more than one. Knowledge contributes reference material. Topics hold authored dialogue. Tools execute defined capabilities. Instructions guide behavior but do not grant data access or guarantee correctness. A conversational trigger and an event trigger are different entry points. This workshop uses the user-message route. The diagram is a simplified conceptual map of the standard harness, not a guaranteed execution sequence.

slides.title: Starting a Copilot Studio trial
lines: Open the official Copilot Studio trial sign-up
Enter a work or school email address
Follow the account-specific sign-up prompts
Open the available authoring environment
slides.notes: Demonstrate the official trial route from the current Microsoft Learn Get access article. The linked sign-up address is https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkId=2107702. Enter a work or school email, select Next, and follow the prompts for that account. Do not invent a universal screen sequence: tenant configuration and existing entitlement change what appears. Use an instructor-controlled account for the demonstration. Learners can watch the full route without creating accounts during class. If the account is already licensed, explain the observed route rather than pretending it is a new trial.

slides.title: Trial access and its limits
lines: What happens | What to do
Work or school identity is required | Use the appropriate organizational account.
Self-service signup is blocked | Use the documented administrator route.
Trial authoring and testing are available | Practice with synthetic course data.
Publishing is unavailable on the trial | Watch the entitled instructor publish demo.

slides.notes: A trial can support authoring and testing, but it cannot publish agents. A personal email or organizational self-service restriction may prevent signup. Show the documented administrator route as a follow-up, not a policy change to perform during class. Trial license and trial environment expiry are different. Inspect the actual expiry notices; do not promise a sixty-day initial period from memory. Save course work through the documented environment process before expiry. The teaching design does not depend on every attendee completing signup today.

Persona and job | A cloud beginner needs supported explanations and practice.
Instructions | Use the course reference. State when it does not support an answer.
Boundary | No exam booking, private policy claims, or pass guarantees.

slides.notes: Read the user and job together. The brief should make a test possible. Ask the class what evidence would distinguish a helpful answer from a confident invention. Our zero-invented-policy target applies to the cases we actually run; it is not a guarantee about every future response. Save the brief before opening authoring controls. A small topic and tool inventory makes it easier to understand which capability was selected.

slides.title: One map, five purposes
lines: Purpose | Course implementation
Overview | Grounded explanation from the course reference
Practice | One authored teach-question-feedback topic
Study plan | GetStudySession flow
Fallback | Honest limitation and mentor referral
Search | Knowledge retrieval with source inspection
slides.notes: A purpose on a topic map does not require a separate authored topic. Overview and search can use grounded answers. Practice needs a controlled dialogue because we must wait for new learner thinking. Study planning uses the tool introduced in Extend. Fallback explains what the agent could not do and offers a truthful next step. We explicitly author the practice sequence and inspect the fallback path. Descriptions must distinguish these purposes so orchestration has useful choices.

slides.title: The shell and the first boundary
lines: Demo: blank agent, instructions, orchestration
Test: “What is my exact exam appointment?”
Your decision: one topic, one instruction, one metric
slides.notes: Use the Inception guide to create a blank agent in the documented standard experience. Review the actual orchestration setting and approved model. Save the instructions, then run the appointment prompt in a fresh conversation. The source cannot know this personal fact. Inspect the response rather than assuming the instruction worked. This is an instructor demonstration. Learners write one instruction, one topic purpose, and one metric without needing an account. Trial setup and account approval never consume the whole segment.

slides.title: 10-minute break
lines: Return at 10:00 AM Central
Build: the source and the conversation
slides.notes: Pause the teaching clock for the scheduled ten-minute break.

slides.title: The source behind an answer
lines: Question
Retrieve relevant passage
Generate an answer
Inspect answer and source
slides.notes: Grounding supplies evidence from a reference at response time. Use the original Contoso Azure concepts file so we can inspect a small, known source. The file is course-authored teaching material grounded in Microsoft Learn, not a Microsoft publication or a complete exam syllabus. Ask who patches the guest operating system on a Contoso Azure virtual machine. Compare the generated answer with the supporting passage. An attached citation is something to inspect; it is not an accuracy certificate. Test the unsupported appointment question separately. The diagram explains retrieval conceptually, not a promise that every answer follows this path.

slides.title: Knowledge scope and limits
lines: Choice | Consequence for this assistant
Agent knowledge | A shared reference for general study questions
Topic grounding | A selected source scope for a particular conversation
Source order | No “first uploaded source wins” rule
Limits and citations | Check source readiness, scope, and the supporting passage
slides.notes: Agent-level knowledge is available broadly. A generative answers node can use an explicit selected-source scope; inspect its Search only selected sources setting. Do not teach upload order as source priority. Names and descriptions help selection. For this controlled build, turn off broad web search and ungrounded responses, then test. These settings have limitations and do not guarantee every claim is correct. The instructor guide records current size and source-count limits with the relevant docs. One small text file is a teaching choice that reduces setup and processing time, not a product limit.

slides.title: Teach, wait, then give feedback
lines: Message: teach the concept
Question: WAIT for a choice
Correct choice: explain why
Incorrect choice: explain misconception
Unmatched twice: offer recovery
slides.notes: A question mark in a Message node does not make the agent wait. Use a Question node with native multiple-choice options and a saved response variable. Configure Ask every time because a practice answer must come from the learner now, rather than from an earlier conversation. The correct branch and incorrect branches must explain different things. An unmatched answer needs an honest recovery. Test the first turn to see that the answer key is withheld, then reply to verify feedback. Our authored lesson is a controlled message; the separate source test demonstrates generative retrieval.

slides.title: Context reuse or a new answer?
lines: Situation | Use
“Give me a cloud study session” | Dynamically fill the tool/topic input from context
Assistant asks: “Who patches the guest OS?” | Question node; wait for the learner’s choice
A required value is missing | Prompt for it; do not guess
An answer does not match | One reprompt, then a truthful recovery
slides.notes: Automatic input filling is useful when the conversation already tells us the desired study focus. It is the wrong substitute for a new quiz response. The proposal uses the term AutomaticTaskInput. The current documented authoring behavior is Dynamically fill with the best option, with a separate Should prompt user control. We teach those documented controls without asserting that the proposal term is a current UI label or fabricating its YAML. Show the distinction on an input and on a Question node, then return to the instructor demonstration.

slides.title: The practice topic, built together
lines: Watch: lesson → Question node → feedback
Predict the next turn before I run it
Identify the wait point and explain one wrong-answer branch
slides.notes: The instructor authors and tests the practice topic while learners predict its behavior. Pause before the first test: should the assistant reveal the answer now? Use the seven-minute universal exercise in the Build guide. Learners sketch or annotate the node sequence and explain the feedback for an incorrect choice. No tenant account is required. Show the actual wait, feedback, and unmatched-answer recovery, then compare those observations with predictions. The full lab remains available for optional independent practice after class. Do not report design work as proof of independent authoring.

slides.title: A useful failure response
lines: Unsupported: “I do not have your exam appointment.”
Recovery: “Check your booking confirmation.”
Human boundary: “I cannot contact a mentor from here.”
slides.notes: A failure response should identify the missing support and give a next step that actually exists. Inspect both the authored topic’s recovery and the system fallback route. Instructions alone do not change a system fallback message. A topic named Escalate does not prove anyone was contacted. Use the fallback and escalation instructions in the guide to avoid promising a transfer. Debrief the demonstration results: source passage, wait point, branch-specific feedback, and the observed limitation. Ask which of those we would lose if we only watched a polished final chat.

slides.title: 10-minute break
lines: Return at 11:00 AM Central
Extend: one useful tool
slides.notes: Pause the teaching clock for the scheduled ten-minute break.

slides.title: The next action
lines: User request | Appropriate next step
Explain shared responsibility | Answer using knowledge
Give me a study session; focus unspecified | Clarify the focus
Give me the cloud study session | Call GetStudySession
Book my exam or decide an accommodation | Refer to an authorized human or service
slides.notes: The right response depends on the job. Use these requests to distinguish generating a supported answer from collecting information or running an operation. Our tool retrieves a fixed, reviewed session so we can see an unambiguous capability boundary. It does not write to an external system. Ask why a booking request belongs outside this assistant’s authority. Keep the tool demonstration about input, execution, and evidence rather than adding a connector to make it look impressive.

slides.title: GetStudySession: the contract
lines: Input: focus
GetStudySession native agent flow
Outputs: status and plan, both Text
slides.notes: The input is one Text value: cloud, security, or governance. These are course focus codes, not the official exam domain names. The outputs are status and plan, both Text. A valid focus returns ok and a reviewed thirty-minute session. An unsupported nonempty focus value such as quantum returns unsupported and a choice reminder. Runtime failure is different from an unsupported value. The flow never books, mails, or updates a record. This is a real tool pattern once the native flow is built and bound; the authored JSON fixture alone is not a deployed flow.

slides.title: The flow behind the tool
lines: Agent calls flow
Initialize status and plan
If cloud
If security
If governance
Respond once
slides.notes: A tool is the capability the agent can call. The agent flow implements that capability, and the designer’s actions are steps inside it. Follow the native recipe: When an agent calls the flow, initialize String variables for status and plan at the top level, evaluate three conditions, and respond once after the branches. Keep the default unsupported response unless a supported focus matches. The native response is synchronous and must meet the documented timeout. We do not need loops, arrays, or a hosted API to teach this first boundary.

slides.title: The evidence of a tool call
lines: Expected input: focus = cloud
Expected output: status = ok; plan describes 30 minutes
No execution record? The response alone is insufficient.
slides.notes: Use the actual prepared native flow and agent binding from the Extend guide. Run the direct flow test, then request the cloud session through the agent. Inspect the actual input and returned status and plan in the available activity view. Count the plan allocation: ten minutes reading, ten explaining, five recall, and five checking. Test unsupported input and tool unavailability as separate conditions. These slide values describe the expected contract, not results we observed while writing the course. If using a rehearsal recording, identify it as recorded before playing it.

slides.title: HTTP and MCP
lines: Mechanism | What the maker needs to understand
HTTP tool | A defined endpoint, request contract, and response
MCP server | Available capabilities, their descriptions, and server access
Both | Identity, permitted data, errors, and approval
This workshop | One native agent flow; other mechanisms are comparisons
slides.notes: HTTP lets a tool call a defined web operation. MCP provides a protocol for exposing discoverable tools and resources through a server. The reviewed Copilot Studio MCP integration requires generative orchestration. Neither supplies permission merely by being connected. For Contoso, a future approved learning catalog might offer one HTTP operation or an MCP server with several described tools. We do not build either integration in this first tool lesson. The learner needs to explain which boundary it introduces and which identity calls it. Keep authentication, endpoint restrictions, and data policy in the decision.

slides.title: When another agent helps
lines: Parent agent
Child agent: specialized work
Connected agent: separately managed
A2A: a protocol for agent communication
slides.notes: Keep our small study assistant as one agent. Add specialization only when another agent has a distinct job or owner. A child agent is organized within a parent. A connected agent can be managed separately. A2A describes an interoperability protocol rather than a third ownership model. Current Microsoft guidance also lists connections involving Microsoft Foundry, Fabric, and Microsoft 365 Agents SDK. Their prerequisites and availability differ. They are extension awareness here, not working course integrations. Ask learners what new responsibility would justify another agent and how they would test the handoff.

slides.title: Authority and human handoff
lines: Claim | Evidence required
“Contact your mentor” | A truthful route the user can take
“I submitted your request” | A real authorized operation and returned receipt
“You are connected to a person” | A supported handoff and accepted transfer
“The tool can access this data” | The intended identity and policy allow that access
slides.notes: Do not confuse a friendly sentence with a completed business operation. A referral tells the user where to go. Submitting a request requires a real, authorized connector and evidence of successful submission. A live transfer requires a supported integration and an accepted handoff. Our course agent only offers a mentor referral. The same distinction applies to authentication: instructions cannot grant permissions. Check the execution identity, connector policy, and allowed data before adding tools or external models. Use synthetic training content for the exercise.

slides.title: Your tool decision
lines: For Contoso: name the input and expected output
Distinguish an unsupported focus from an unavailable tool
Name one request that needs a human
slides.notes: Give everyone three minutes to reason through the same Contoso contract. No account or flow attachment is required. Ask for the input, two output fields, and an unsupported request. The instructor then uses the prepared agent and native flow to inspect real execution evidence and revisit failures. Predictions stay labeled as predictions until observed. The independent tool lab remains optional after class.

slides.title: Two evaluation sets, two questions
lines: Prepared set | Question it answers

AZ900-live-three
Compare meaning: E04, E05, E08 | Does the response match the expected meaning?

AZ900-tool-one
Tool use: E08 only | Did it use the actual GetStudySession capability?
Separate manual conversation | Did the topic wait, then give the correct feedback?
slides.notes: Start with prepared native sets to protect time for interpreting results. AZ900-live-three uses Compare meaning for E04, E05, and E08, each with an expected response. AZ900-tool-one uses Tool use only for E08 and selects the actual GetStudySession capability. Remove the default General quality method when configuring these deliberately focused sets. Methods are configured on the set. Leaving expected tools blank on the other two cases would produce Invalid results for that method, not a clean skip. The eighty-percent meaning threshold is an initial course choice, not a Microsoft recommendation. Single-response grading does not simulate answering the quiz; the wait and feedback still need a manual multi-turn test.

slides.title: A score and an execution trace
lines: Same test set
Run before
One change
Run after
Compare individual cases
Inspect source and tool trace
slides.notes: Run the same prepared set before and after one change. Open a failed case, read the expected and actual response, then inspect the activity map for the supporting knowledge or tool call. A generated grading rationale can be wrong, so verify the underlying evidence. Compare the same set, not different questions with convenient scores. If changing the agent model, record the approved configuration and rerun the same cases. Primary orchestration and individual prompt-model settings are distinct. Export genuine results using the documented control; never substitute the authored expectations for an executed report.

slides.title: Usage signals need interpretation
lines: Signal | What it does and does not tell us
10 sessions: 9 did not escalate | 90% containment proxy
6 resolved; 3 abandoned; 1 escalated | 60% resolution; 30% abandonment
4 survey responses | The survey describes those 4 respondents
High containment and wrong answers | Inspect outcomes, transcripts, and source evidence together
slides.notes: This is synthetic discussion data, not tenant telemetry. In the guide’s ten-session example, nine sessions did not escalate, but only six resolved. Three were abandoned and one escalated. A ninety-percent containment proxy therefore coexists with sixty-percent resolution. The survey describes its four respondents, not every user. Show a genuine prepared channel analytics sample separately. Test-panel traffic is excluded from Monitor, and channel data can arrive with a delay. Inspect confirmed and implied resolution, abandonment, transcripts, user feedback, and response time together. Our classroom containment proxy is not a claimed native metric name.

slides.title: Five Well-Architected concerns
lines: Concern | Control for the study assistant
Reliability | Tool failure has a clear recovery path.
Security | Use the intended identity and approved sources.
Operational Excellence | An owner reviews repeatable tests and incidents.
Performance Efficiency | Measure response time and unnecessary tool work.
Experience Optimization | Wait for the learner; give useful feedback and a next step.
slides.notes: Use the Power Platform framework rather than reciting five labels. Reliability means useful recovery when a tool is unavailable. Security means an approved identity and permitted data. Operational excellence means repeatable tests and an owner who can respond. Performance efficiency means measuring the response and tool behavior instead of assuming a longer answer is better. Experience optimization means the learner sees useful feedback, understands a limitation, and can reach a real next step. These are course examples of the framework, not a Microsoft certification of our agent.

slides.title: Publishing and audience access
lines: Tested draft
Publish configured version
Scoped channel and access
Fresh session with actual user
slides.notes: Publishing makes the configured version available to connected channels; it does not by itself establish who can use it. Use an entitled instructor environment, a prepared scoped Teams channel, and a fresh conversation. Demonstrate one publish operation and two short checks, with a second-user access check prepared separately. Do not ask trial-only learners to publish: current licensing guidance permits trial creation and testing but not publication. Development, test, and production separation, data policy, and an approved audience remain part of rollout planning. An installation link is not evidence that access was granted.

slides.title: Channel choice changes the checks
lines: Channel | Preparation to verify
Teams: course demonstration | Entitlement, scoped access, installation, fresh conversation
SharePoint: comparison | Site permission, published agent, allowed deployment
Microsoft 365 Copilot: comparison | Channel configuration and approved audience
Every channel | Actual user access, source permissions, and behavior
slides.notes: Teams is the live course channel. SharePoint and Microsoft 365 Copilot are scoped comparisons. Each route has its own setup, permissions, and availability. For SharePoint, the maker needs the documented site access and deployment prerequisites. For Microsoft 365 Copilot, inspect the channel configuration and approved audience rather than assuming the Teams configuration enables every surface. Test fresh conversation behavior and the actual intended user. Never use a public channel as a workaround for a blocked private pilot.

slides.title: Your pilot decision
lines: Name one agent worth piloting
Choose its users, owner, data boundary, and stop condition
Cite one result and label its evidence source
slides.notes: Protect seven minutes for the Operate worksheet. A useful decision could be a small internal training pilot with approved content and a named owner. Learners should identify what would stop the pilot, not only what would start it. Use the synthetic case if real observations are unavailable, and label the evidence accordingly. A worksheet is evidence of reasoning; it is not evidence that publishing or evaluation executed. Invite one learner to challenge another pilot’s boundary using the five concerns.

slides.title: The same pattern at work
lines: Course component | Workplace transfer
Azure reference | Approved internal knowledge
Practice topic | A controlled training or triage interaction
Study-session tool | One bounded lookup or operation
Pilot decision | Named audience, owner, evidence, and stop condition
slides.notes: Transfer the architecture rather than copying the Azure subject. A help-desk agent could ground answers in approved support articles, use a topic for triage, and call an approved lookup. An onboarding assistant might ground in approved guidance and refer a sensitive case to a person. Each new scenario needs its own access and evaluation cases. For follow-up, inspect a genuine topic capture in the native code editor or VS Code. YAML represents authored structure; it is not a magic portable deployment. The export guide explains the procedure. The actual sanitized capture must come from the teaching tenant before it is distributed.

slides.title: The four outcomes in practice
lines: Plan: a brief with a testable boundary
Build: source evidence and a topic that waits
Extend: a tool contract and a human boundary
Operate: test evidence and a defensible pilot decision
slides.notes: Return to the four advertised outcomes and invite learners to explain the evidence shown. Their brief, topic prediction, tool decision, and pilot decision are useful learning artifacts even without tenant access. The supplied steps let them repeat the build when a trial or approved environment is available. A blocked operation remains unrun; a prediction does not count as a successful tenant test. Use the remaining wrap-up time for questions and one follow-up practice commitment.
